source.title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of How to Win Friends and Influence People by Dale Carnegie (1936). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary; contains no text from the book. In copyright in the US until 2032 (1936, renewed); public domain since 2026 in life+70 countries (Carnegie died 1955). Summarised so cards are safe everywhere.

cards.title: Criticism usually backfires because people defend themselves
cards.body:
Carnegie noticed that almost nobody sees themselves as the villain. Even people who have done real harm tend to have a story that justifies what they did. So when you criticise someone, they rarely reflect; they dig in, feel hurt, and may resent you for years.

His advice is to hold back the urge to blame and instead try to understand why the person acted as they did. Today that applies to code reviews, family arguments and comment sections alike: a sharp put-down feels good for a moment but almost never changes behaviour.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel the urge to criticise someone, pause and write down one reason their choice might have made sense to them.

quiz.question: Why does Carnegie think criticism rarely changes people?
options: People don't hear it
It is usually wrong
People forget it quickly
It makes them defensive and they justify themselves
quiz.explanation: Most people see their own actions as justified, so criticism triggers self-defence rather than reflection.

cards.title: People hunger to feel valued, so give real appreciation
cards.body:
A central idea in the book is that a deep human need is to feel important and noticed. Carnegie argues that sincere appreciation is one of the most powerful things you can offer, and one of the rarest.

He draws a sharp line between this and flattery. Flattery is cheap, vague and self-serving, and people can smell it. Genuine appreciation is specific and honest: you name something the person actually did well. In a workplace where most feedback points out problems, a precise thank-you stands out and builds lasting goodwill.
cards.apply_it: Send one message today thanking someone for a specific thing they did, saying exactly what it was and why it helped.

quiz.question: How does Carnegie distinguish appreciation from flattery?
options: Flattery is more effective at work
There is no real difference
Appreciation is sincere and specific; flattery is insincere
Appreciation should only come from managers
quiz.explanation: He saw honest, specific appreciation as valuable and flattery as hollow and easily detected.

cards.title: To persuade someone, start with what they want
cards.body:
Carnegie points out that people are mostly interested in their own goals, not yours. When you go fishing, you bait the hook with what the fish likes, not with what you like to eat.

The same applies to persuasion. Instead of explaining why you want something, show how it helps the other person get what they care about. A manager asking for overtime, a parent asking a teenager to tidy up or a founder pitching investors will get further by framing the request around the other side's interests.
cards.apply_it: Before your next request, write one sentence describing what the other person gains from saying yes, and lead with it.

quiz.question: What is Carnegie's starting point for influencing someone?
options: Explain your own needs clearly
Talk about what the other person wants
Repeat your request until they agree
Offer a reward up front
quiz.explanation: People respond to their own interests, so frame requests around what they care about.

cards.title: Remembering someone's name is a small act of respect
cards.body:
Carnegie stresses how much people care about their own names. Using someone's name correctly tells them they registered with you; forgetting or misspelling it quietly signals that they didn't.

He describes successful people who made a deliberate effort to remember the names of those they met. It is a skill, not a talent: repeat the name when you hear it, use it in conversation and connect it to something memorable. In a world of video calls and big teams, getting names right is an easy way to make people feel seen.
cards.apply_it: In your next introduction, repeat the person's name back once and use it again before you part. Jot it down afterwards.

quiz.question: According to Carnegie, why does remembering names matter?
options: It shows people they matter to you
It helps you win arguments
It is required by etiquette
It makes you seem clever
quiz.explanation: A person's own name matters a lot to them, so using it signals respect and attention.

cards.title: Be curious about others and let them do the talking
cards.body:
Carnegie's view is that showing real interest in other people builds friendships far faster than working to make them interested in you.

A big part of this is listening. Ask questions people enjoy answering, encourage them to talk about their work and passions, and resist steering everything back to yourself. People often leave such conversations thinking you were great company, even if you said very little. The key word is genuine: curiosity that is faked to get something tends to show.
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation, ask two follow-up questions about something the other person cares about before sharing your own view.

quiz.question: What does Carnegie suggest is the quickest way to make friends?
options: Tell impressive stories
Agree with everything they say
Give gifts
Show genuine interest in other people and listen
quiz.explanation: Real interest in others, shown by listening and asking questions, builds connection faster than trying to impress.

cards.title: Nobody really wins an argument, so avoid them and admit mistakes fast
cards.body:
Carnegie's view is that arguments are almost unwinnable. Even if you prove your point, the other person feels beaten and believes their view more firmly than before. You have won the debate and lost the relationship.

He recommends respecting the other person's opinion, avoiding blunt statements that they are wrong, and, when you are the one in error, owning it quickly and openly. Admitting a mistake before anyone has to point it out disarms people and often makes them more generous. It is a useful antidote to online pile-ons and heated meetings.
cards.apply_it: The next time you realise you got something wrong, say so first and plainly, before anyone else raises it.

quiz.question: Why does Carnegie say you can't win an argument?
options: Facts never matter
Arguments are always too long
The loser usually resents it and holds their view more strongly
Someone else always interrupts
quiz.explanation: Beating someone in an argument tends to harden their position and damage the relationship.

cards.title: Correct people gently and let them keep their dignity
cards.body:
When someone needs to change, Carnegie suggests a softer route than direct reproach. Begin with honest praise, point to the problem indirectly, and mention mistakes you have made yourself so the other person doesn't feel singled out.

Above all, let them save face. Humiliating someone, even when you are right, can leave a lasting wound and kill their motivation. Asking questions instead of giving orders, and making the fix seem easy to achieve, helps people improve while keeping their self-respect intact.
cards.apply_it: Before giving feedback, start with one sincere positive and share a time you made a similar mistake.

quiz.question: What does Carnegie recommend when you need to correct someone?
options: Be blunt so the message is clear
Let them save face and point to mistakes indirectly
Correct them in front of others
Wait for them to notice on their own
quiz.explanation: Preserving dignity and approaching mistakes indirectly makes people more willing to change.

cards.title: A genuine smile tells people you're glad to see them
cards.body:
Carnegie argues that a real smile is one of the cheapest and most effective ways to make people like you. It signals, before you say a word, that you are pleased to be with them. He is clear that a forced, mechanical grin does the opposite: people can tell the difference.

He adds that the warmth carries even when people can't see you, for example in your tone on a phone call. In a busy office, a shop or a family home, greeting people as if you're happy they're there sets the mood for everything that follows.
cards.apply_it: Tomorrow, greet the first three people you meet with a real smile and a warm hello, and notice how they respond.

quiz.question: What kind of smile does Carnegie say wins people over?
options: A genuine smile that shows you're glad to see them
A wide smile held throughout the conversation
A polite smile used only with important people
No smile, because it looks unserious
quiz.explanation: Carnegie values sincere warmth; a forced smile backfires.

cards.title: Act cheerful and the feeling often follows
cards.body:
Carnegie leans on the psychologist William James for a practical point: feeling and action tend to move together. We can't always order a feeling to change, but we can change what we do, and the feeling often follows. So if you feel low or awkward, he suggests behaving as though you were already in good spirits.

Carnegie also argues that happiness depends less on what you have or where you are than on how you think about it. This isn't a cure for real depression, but for everyday gloom it is a useful lever you control.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel flat before a meeting or visit, stand tall, smile and speak with energy for the first minute. Notice whether your mood shifts.

quiz.question: According to the idea Carnegie borrows from William James, how can you influence a feeling?
options: By waiting until it passes on its own
By arguing yourself out of it
By changing your actions, since feeling tends to follow
By talking about it with as many people as possible
quiz.explanation: Action is more under our control than feeling, and feeling tends to follow action.

cards.title: Talk about what the other person cares about
cards.body:
Carnegie describes how admired figures, such as Theodore Roosevelt, would read up on a visitor's interests before meeting them, so the conversation could begin with something that person loved.

The principle is simple: the quickest way into someone's heart is to talk about the things they treasure most. Rather than opening with your own news or agenda, find out what excites them: their children, their farm, their football club, their side business. People rarely forget someone who took real interest in what matters to them, and it often makes the rest of the conversation easier.
cards.apply_it: Before your next important meeting, find out one thing the other person is passionate about, and ask them about it early.

quiz.question: Why did Carnegie admire visitors being greeted with talk about their own interests?
options: Because the quickest way to win people is to talk about what they treasure
Because it wastes time and makes meetings shorter
Because it lets you avoid saying anything about yourself forever
Because it impresses people with how much you know
quiz.explanation: Opening with the other person's interests shows real care and builds connection.

cards.title: Make people feel important, and want nothing in return
cards.body:
Carnegie tells of brightening a bored post-office clerk's day with a sincere compliment, wanting nothing from him at all. His point is that the urge to feel important is universal, so we should honour it in everyone we meet, not only in people who can help us.

He recommends small courtesies like 'thank you', 'would you mind' and 'sorry to trouble you'. They oil the wheels of daily life. But the key is motive: kindness offered as a trick to get something soon looks hollow, while kindness given freely leaves a lasting glow on both sides.
cards.apply_it: Today, give one sincere, specific compliment to someone who can do nothing for you, such as a cleaner, driver or shop assistant.

quiz.question: What does Carnegie stress about making others feel important?
options: Only do it with people who can help your career
Do it sincerely, without expecting anything back
Do it with lavish flattery so they notice
Avoid it, since it makes people arrogant
quiz.explanation: Carnegie's example involved wanting nothing from the clerk; sincerity is the point.

cards.title: Greet people warmly and remember the dates that matter to them
cards.body:
In his chapter on being genuinely interested in others, Carnegie mentions habits that cost little but say a lot. He describes collecting friends' birthdays and sending a note or greeting on the day, and greeting people, including on the phone, with an energy that shows you're pleased to hear from them.

These gestures matter because they prove that you thought about someone when you didn't have to. Today a calendar reminder makes this easy, but the message still needs to be personal. A flat 'HBD' says much less than a warm line that shows you know them.
cards.apply_it: Add the birthdays of five people you care about to your calendar, with a reminder to send a personal message.

quiz.question: Why do small gestures like remembering birthdays work, according to the card?
options: They are expected, so skipping them causes offence
They make people owe you a favour
They replace the need for real conversation
They prove you thought about someone when you didn't have to
quiz.explanation: The value is in showing unprompted thoughtfulness.

cards.title: Begin in a friendly way if you want people to listen
cards.body:
Carnegie retells the fable of the sun and the wind competing to make a man take off his coat. The wind blows hard and the man only clutches the coat tighter; the sun shines gently and the coat comes off.

His lesson is that warmth persuades better than force. If you start a difficult conversation angry or hostile, the other person's defences go up at once. Starting in a friendly, respectful way, even when you have a genuine complaint, makes people far more willing to hear you out. A complaint to a landlord, a supplier or a family member lands better this way.
cards.apply_it: Before sending your next complaint message, rewrite the first line so it opens warmly and respectfully.

quiz.question: In the sun and wind fable Carnegie uses, what finally removes the man's coat?
options: The wind blowing harder
The man getting tired
Rain falling on him
The gentle warmth of the sun
quiz.explanation: Gentleness succeeded where force failed.

cards.title: Get early 'yes' answers before raising points of disagreement
cards.body:
Carnegie advises that when you want to persuade someone, you shouldn't start with the issues you disagree on. Begin with the things you both agree about and keep emphasising them, so the person gets into the habit of saying yes.

He links this to the questioning style of Socrates, who led people step by step through points they accepted. Carnegie's reasoning is that once someone has said a firm 'no', pride makes them want to stay consistent with it. Building agreement first keeps minds open for the harder part of the conversation.
cards.apply_it: In your next negotiation, list three things you and the other side already agree on and open with them.

quiz.question: Why does Carnegie warn against getting a 'no' early in a conversation?
options: Because 'no' is rude
Because pride pushes people to stay consistent with their 'no'
Because it ends the conversation by law
Because it means they didn't hear you
quiz.explanation: Once people commit to 'no', they tend to defend it.

cards.title: Let others feel an idea is their own
cards.body:
Carnegie observes that people trust ideas they discover themselves far more than ideas handed to them. So rather than pushing your plan, he suggests offering hints, asking for suggestions and letting the other person arrive at the conclusion.

When a team helps shape a plan, they feel ownership and work harder to make it succeed. This takes patience and some humility, since you may not get the credit. But in workplaces, families and community groups, an idea people feel is theirs usually gets carried out with more energy than an order.
cards.apply_it: For your next proposal, ask the group, 'What do you think we should do about this?' before sharing your own view.

quiz.question: Why does Carnegie suggest letting people feel an idea is theirs?
options: Because it saves you from doing any work
Because ideas from leaders are usually wrong
Because people trust and commit to ideas they discover themselves
Because it lets you blame them if it fails
quiz.explanation: Ownership increases trust and commitment.

cards.title: Before a key conversation, imagine what the other person will say
cards.body:
Carnegie suggests honestly trying to see things from the other person's point of view. He says he would rather pace outside someone's office for a long time than walk in without a clear idea of what he would say and how the other person was likely to respond, given their interests and motives.

This is not mind-reading; it's preparation. When you have considered the other side's worries and reasons in advance, you can address them directly, sound reasonable rather than demanding, and avoid being surprised by objections you could have predicted.
cards.apply_it: Before your next important request, write down the two objections the other person is most likely to raise and how you'd respond.

quiz.question: What did Carnegie want to be clear on before entering an important meeting?
options: Both what he would say and how the other person was likely to respond
Only what he wanted to say
How long the meeting would last
Who else would be in the room
quiz.explanation: He prepared by thinking through the other person's likely view.

cards.title: Tell upset people you'd likely feel the same in their place
cards.body:
Carnegie describes a simple way to calm angry or upset people: acknowledge that, given their situation, you would probably feel exactly as they do. Often this is honestly true, since if you had their background, pressures and information, you might well react the same way.

He argues that most people are hungry for sympathy, and that offering it first defuses hostility far faster than defending yourself. It doesn't mean agreeing with everything they want. It means showing you understand why they feel as they do, which makes them far more willing to listen to your side.
cards.apply_it: Next time someone is upset with you, start with: 'I can see why you'd feel that way.' Then pause and listen.

quiz.question: What does Carnegie suggest saying to someone who is upset?
options: That they are overreacting
That they should calm down first
Nothing until they stop
That you'd likely feel the same in their place
quiz.explanation: Sympathy defuses hostility and opens the door to dialogue.

cards.title: Appeal to people's better motives
cards.body:
Carnegie suggests that people usually have two reasons for doing something: one that sounds good, and the real one. Most of us like to think of ourselves as fair and honourable, so he advises appealing to those finer motives.

His examples involve treating people as honest and decent, for instance asking a tenant or customer to act fairly because you believe they are fair-minded people. Many respond by living up to that picture. It won't work with everyone, but treating people as trustworthy often brings out more of their better side than suspicion does.
cards.apply_it: Next time you need cooperation, frame your request around fairness or integrity, such as 'I know you want to do the right thing here.'

quiz.question: Which motives does Carnegie advise appealing to?
options: Fear of punishment
Greed and personal gain only
People's sense of fairness and honour
Envy of others
quiz.explanation: He suggests that most people want to see themselves as fair and decent.

cards.title: Bring your idea to life instead of just stating it
cards.body:
Carnegie points out that plain facts often aren't enough, because people are busy and distracted. He recommends dramatising ideas: showing them in a vivid, memorable way, as shop windows, advertisers and good salespeople do.

His examples include demonstrations and visual stunts that made a point impossible to ignore. Today that could mean bringing a physical sample to a meeting, showing a simple before-and-after photo, or turning a dull number into a picture people can grasp. The goal is not trickery but making the truth vivid enough to be noticed.
cards.apply_it: For your next pitch or request, plan one visual or hands-on way to show your point, not just say it.

quiz.question: Why does Carnegie recommend dramatising your ideas?
options: Because truth alone is boring and should be exaggerated
Because people are busy, and vivid ideas get noticed and remembered
Because it hides weak arguments
Because people prefer jokes to facts
quiz.explanation: Dramatising makes a true point vivid; it's not about exaggeration.

cards.title: A fair challenge can motivate more than money
cards.body:
Carnegie argues that one of the strongest drivers at work is the desire to excel and prove yourself. He tells of a manager whose mill workers kept missing targets; rather than lecturing, he simply made each shift's output visible, and the shifts began trying to beat each other.

The lesson is that people often rise to a challenge that lets them show what they can do. Done well, this means healthy goals and visible progress, not humiliation. A team that can see its score and wants to beat it usually needs far less pushing.
cards.apply_it: Pick one task your team or household finds dull and make progress visible, such as a simple chart, so people can try to beat their best.

quiz.question: What did Carnegie's mill example use to raise output?
options: Making each shift's output visible so they competed
Cutting wages until targets were met
Threatening to fire the slowest workers
Adding more supervisors
quiz.explanation: Visible results turned the work into a challenge people wanted to win.

cards.title: Praise every small improvement, not just big wins
cards.body:
Carnegie compares people to animals being trained: trainers reward each small step in the right direction, not only the finished trick. He argues that people respond the same way. Noticing and praising even slight progress encourages them to keep going.

The praise must be honest and specific, or it sounds like flattery. Many of us save our compliments for perfection and point out every flaw along the way. Reversing that, so that you spot progress and say so, helps learners, children and new staff build confidence and skill faster.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who is learning something. Today, tell them one specific way they've improved.

quiz.question: According to Carnegie, when should you offer praise?
options: Only when the job is perfect
Never, since it makes people lazy
Only in annual reviews
For every improvement, even slight ones, as long as it's honest
quiz.explanation: Honest praise for small steps encourages continued progress.

cards.title: Give people a good reputation to live up to
cards.body:
When someone's work slips, Carnegie suggests treating them as if they already have the quality you'd like to see. Tell a usually reliable worker that you know they take pride in their work. Many people will try hard not to let that picture down.

He sees this as more effective than labelling someone careless, which tends to confirm the label. The reputation must be believable and offered sincerely; it isn't a trick. But expecting the best from people, out loud, often helps them find it.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone whose performance has dipped. Plan to remind them of a strength you've genuinely seen in them before you raise the issue.

quiz.question: What does Carnegie suggest when someone isn't performing well?
options: Label the problem clearly so they can't deny it
Treat them as already having the quality you want to see
Ignore it and hope it improves
Compare them with better colleagues
quiz.explanation: A believable good reputation gives people something to live up to.

cards.title: Make people glad to do what you ask
cards.body:
Carnegie suggests that when you ask someone to do something, you think about what's in it for them and present it in a way that makes them happy to take part. He mentions how leaders like Napoleon handed out titles and honours that cost little but made people proud.

In practice, that means being sincere, explaining the benefit to the person, giving them real responsibility and matching the request to their interests. Someone given a meaningful role, rather than a dull order, usually works with more pride and better results.
cards.apply_it: Before delegating your next task, name one honest way it benefits or recognises the person, and mention it when you ask.

quiz.question: What is the aim of this principle?
options: To trick people into extra work
To pay people more for every task
To present requests so people are happy to take part
To avoid giving people any responsibility
quiz.explanation: Carnegie wants people to feel proud and glad, not cornered.

cards.title: Swap 'but' for 'and' when giving feedback
cards.body:
In discussing how to point out mistakes indirectly, Carnegie notes a common trap: praising someone and then saying 'but'. The listener hears the praise as a set-up and stops believing it.

His suggestion is to link the praise and the suggestion with 'and' instead. 'You've improved a lot this term, and if you keep practising your maths, your results will rise further' feels like encouragement, not a hidden attack. It's a tiny change of word, but it changes how feedback is received at work, at school and at home.
cards.apply_it: Look at the last piece of feedback you wrote. If it contains 'but' after praise, rewrite it using 'and'.

quiz.question: What happens, according to Carnegie, when praise is followed by 'but'?
options: The listener doubts the praise and hears only criticism
The listener feels doubly encouraged
The feedback becomes more precise
Nothing changes
quiz.explanation: 'But' turns praise into a set-up for criticism.

cards.title: Nagging wears a relationship down
cards.body:
In a section on happier home life, included in the book's original edition, Carnegie warns that constant nagging is among the most destructive habits in marriage. It rarely gets the change you want and slowly poisons the affection between you.

The same applies to parents, flatmates and colleagues. Repeating the same complaint makes the other person defensive and resentful. Carnegie's broader principles offer better tools: appreciation, asking rather than ordering, and making requests in terms of what the other person wants.
cards.apply_it: Notice one complaint you've repeated to a family member. Try raising it once, calmly, as a request, then stop repeating it for a week.

quiz.question: What does Carnegie say constant nagging does in a relationship?
options: It gets results quickly
It is harmless if you are right
It works best with children
It rarely brings change and erodes affection
quiz.explanation: Nagging damages affection without producing change.

cards.title: Don't try to remake the people you love
cards.body:
Also in his advice on home life, Carnegie cautions against trying to change a partner into someone else. Constant attempts to remodel how they talk, dress or think tell them they are not good enough as they are.

This doesn't mean ignoring real problems or harm. It means accepting a person's basic temperament and quirks, and treating them with the same respect you'd give a friend. People tend to grow more when they feel accepted than when they feel under constant renovation.
cards.apply_it: Write down one habit of a loved one you've been trying to change. Ask yourself honestly whether it truly matters, or whether you can let it be.

quiz.question: What message does constantly trying to change a partner send, according to the card?
options: That you care deeply
That they aren't good enough as they are
That you are a good teacher
That they should be more independent
quiz.explanation: Attempts to remodel someone signal disapproval of who they are.

cards.title: Small, regular attentions keep love alive
cards.body:
Carnegie's advice on home life includes paying 'little attentions': the small, everyday signs of thought that are easy to stop doing after years together. He notes that many people only bring flowers or show special care when a partner is sick.

His point is that affection is kept alive by frequent small acts, not occasional grand ones. A quick message during the day, remembering a worry they mentioned, or a small treat for no reason tells someone they're still on your mind.
cards.apply_it: Do one small, unprompted kindness for your partner or a close family member today.

quiz.question: What does Carnegie suggest keeps affection alive at home?
options: Expensive gifts on special occasions
Avoiding each other to prevent arguments
Frequent small signs of thought and care
Only attention when someone is ill
quiz.explanation: Small, regular attentions matter more than rare big gestures.

cards.title: Read with a question: how will I use this?
cards.body:
At the start of the book, Carnegie gives suggestions for getting the most out of it. A key one: as you read, stop often and ask yourself how and when you could apply each idea. He also recommends rereading chapters and marking important passages.

His view is that knowledge only matters when it turns into action. Reading self-help without changing anything is like reading about swimming and never getting in the water. Turning each idea into a specific situation from your own life makes it far more likely you'll use it.
cards.apply_it: After reading this card, write down one specific conversation this week where you'll use a Carnegie principle.

quiz.question: What does Carnegie suggest asking yourself while reading the book?
options: How and when can I apply this idea?
How quickly can I finish this?
Who else needs to read this?
Do I agree with every word?
quiz.explanation: Applying ideas, not just knowing them, is the goal.

cards.title: Review your week: what went well with people, and what didn't
cards.body:
Carnegie describes a businessman who set aside time each week to go through his meetings and conversations, asking what mistakes he made, what he did right and what he could learn. Carnegie recommends a similar weekly check-up on how you're using the book's principles.

Regular reflection turns experience into learning. Without it, we repeat the same social mistakes for years without noticing. A short, honest weekly review, perhaps on a Sunday evening, helps you see patterns in how you treat people and make steady improvements.
cards.apply_it: This weekend, spend ten minutes listing your key conversations this week. Note one thing you handled well and one you'd do differently.

quiz.question: What habit does Carnegie recommend for improving your people skills?
options: A regular weekly review of your conversations and mistakes
A yearly resolution list
Asking friends to rate you online
Avoiding difficult people altogether
quiz.explanation: Regular reflection helps you learn from experience.

cards.title: Ask someone to catch you when you slip
cards.body:
Another of Carnegie's suggestions for practising the book is to turn it into a game. He proposes giving a friend or family member permission to point out whenever you break one of the principles, with a small playful penalty each time.

The idea is that we often can't see our own habits, such as interrupting, criticising or talking only about ourselves. Someone close to you can. Making it a light game keeps it friendly, and the outside eye speeds up change far more than good intentions alone.
cards.apply_it: Choose one habit you want to break, like interrupting. Ask a friend to point it out each time this week, with a small fun forfeit.

quiz.question: Why does Carnegie suggest inviting someone to point out your slips?
options: To make them feel superior
Because others can see habits we can't see in ourselves
Because rules only work with punishment
To avoid having to change at all
quiz.explanation: An outside observer catches habits we miss.
